quotes.text: When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed.

An agent harness—also commonly referred to as an agentic harness— is a software environment that surrounds an artificial intelligence model, giving it the ability to interact with outside tools, remember past interactions, and execute multi-step tasks.
Agent behavior is stochastic: LLM-powered decisions are inherently non-deterministic, the same input might produce different outputs across invocations.
Operational and policy boundaries for each agent are defined up front and enforced through layered controls rather than prompt instructions alone.
Evaluation datasets, prompts, and scoring rubrics are versioned and kept current as agent capabilities and use cases evolve.
Retries are applied without idempotency guarantees, so recovery from transient failures creates duplicate transactions, corrupted state, or silent inconsistency.
Agent reasoning cycles are bounded by explicit termination conditions and confidence-based exits, so token consumption is predictable and proportional to decision complexity.
Zero trust assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location
The actor_token request parameter, however, does provide a means for providing information about the desired actor
Agent executions produce distributed traces that capture reasoning steps, tool invocations, memory operations, and inter-agent handoffs, with trace context propagated across every service boundary.
Agents operate under service identities that are distinct from human identities, and audit trails attribute every action unambiguously to either an agent or a human actor.

Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction.
